Presets: a published dataset's columns onto a generic function's arguments

Source: R/clprep.R
clprep.Rd

A preset says how the columns of one published dataset (an Ontario segregation table, the Special Investigations Unit's cases, a use-of-force file) feed the arguments of one of crimlab's generic functions, so that generic(clprep(data, preset)) gives the published analysis while the same generic runs on anyone's data given as plain vectors. A preset describes a layout and ships no data: the user supplies the table.

Usage

clprep(data = NULL, preset = NULL)

Arguments

data

The dataset: a data frame with the columns the preset names. NULL (with preset NULL) lists the presets.

preset

The preset's name, as clprep() lists them, or a preset of one's own: a data frame of rows laid out as those of presets.tsv (preset, generic and arg needed, the other columns optional); NULL for the list.

Value

With a preset, an object of class clpre: a list of the generic's arguments, which the generic takes as its first argument, with attributes preset, generic, source, units, note and drop. Without one, a data frame of the presets: preset, generic, args and source.

Details

The presets are rows of presets.tsv (in the installed package's presets folder), one per preset and argument: preset, generic, arg, column (the dataset's column), recode, filter, units, note, source. Python reads the same file. A recode is one of: empty (the column as it is); fac (a factor, one effect per value); num (numbers); pct (numbers over 100); one (a 1 for every row); flag (1 for yes, y, true, t, 1 or a positive number, 0 otherwise); dum (one 0 or 1 column per value but the first, named by the column and the value); sub:a,b (characters a to b, as a year from an ISO date); const:v (the argument is v, a number when it reads as one, no column); or a mapping x|y=1;has:abc=1;*=0 from labels, compared without case or surrounding space (has: a label containing the text), to values, * covering every other label and *=NA dropping those rows. A filter col=value keeps the rows whose column has that value. An argument given by several rows (or by dum) is a data frame of their columns, as adj always is. An arg of recipe derives columns first, in the order of the rows: keep drops the rows missing any of the columns named in recode; long stacks the two count columns named in recode as count with with 1 for the first; acvm and pyr reduce one row per placement to one per person and year (see Details of the returned attributes), and acnv does so the naive way (acn, the most alert flags on one row; vmany, 1 when any row changes region; hiacn, acn >= 2); pairb adds tb (two or more of the three alert flags) and yb (Number_Of_Placements of 2 or more); pairc adds tc (the region at placement differs from the most recent) and yc (NumberConsecutiveDays_Segregation capped at its 99th percentile); gent takes the columns inc,rent,colg,rentg named in recode (and optionally the two quantiles, 0.5,0.667 by default) and adds gent, a factor: ineligible unless baseline income and rent are both at most their first quantile, then gentrified when the growth in college graduates and in rent both reach their second quantile, else eligible; pop takes count;rate;per (separated by semicolons, as column names may hold commas) and adds pop, the population count / rate * per that a published rate implies.

Rows with a missing value in any column the preset reads are dropped, as the source analyses drop them; their number is the attribute drop.

Examples

head(clprep())
#>         preset generic               args
#> 1 otis-b03-cnt  cntreg y grp adj clus gee
#> 2 otis-b04-cnt  cntreg          y grp adj
#> 3 otis-b06-cnt  cntreg y grp adj clus gee
#> 4 otis-b07-cnt  cntreg   recipe y grp adj
#> 5 otis-b08-cnt  cntreg y grp adj clus gee
#> 6 otis-b09-cnt  cntreg          y grp adj
#>                                                                                                                        source
#> 1 Ontario Ministry of the Solicitor General, segregation and restrictive confinement data (Ontario Data Catalogue), table b03
#> 2 Ontario Ministry of the Solicitor General, segregation and restrictive confinement data (Ontario Data Catalogue), table b04
#> 3 Ontario Ministry of the Solicitor General, segregation and restrictive confinement data (Ontario Data Catalogue), table b06
#> 4 Ontario Ministry of the Solicitor General, segregation and restrictive confinement data (Ontario Data Catalogue), table b07
#> 5 Ontario Ministry of the Solicitor General, segregation and restrictive confinement data (Ontario Data Catalogue), table b08
#> 6 Ontario Ministry of the Solicitor General, segregation and restrictive confinement data (Ontario Data Catalogue), table b09
# a table laid out as the published OTIS c01 table (numbers made up)
d <- data.frame(EndFiscalYear = rep(2020:2022, each = 2),
                Gender = rep(c("Female", "Male"), 3),
                NumberIndividuals_RestrictiveConfinement =
                  c(40, 310, 52, 335, 47, 360))
p <- clprep(d, "otis-c01-cnt")
cntreg(p)
#> cntreg: 6 counts; reference 0
#> rate ratios (95% intervals):
#>   fit term       irr        lo        hi             p   sep
#>  pois    1 0.1383085 0.1158296 0.1651497 6.153279e-106 FALSE
#>    nb    1 0.1383085 0.1158295 0.1651499 6.174131e-106 FALSE
#> negative binomial theta 7655874; AIC Poisson 48.8636, negative binomial 50.86374
# the same model on plain vectors
cntreg(d$NumberIndividuals_RestrictiveConfinement, d$Gender == "Female",
       adj = factor(d$EndFiscalYear))
#> cntreg: 6 counts; reference FALSE
#> rate ratios (95% intervals):
#>   fit term       irr        lo        hi             p   sep
#>  pois TRUE 0.1383085 0.1158296 0.1651497 6.153279e-106 FALSE
#>    nb TRUE 0.1383085 0.1158295 0.1651499 6.174131e-106 FALSE
#> negative binomial theta 7655874; AIC Poisson 48.8636, negative binomial 50.86374
# a preset of one's own, for another agency's columns
mine <- data.frame(preset = "my-cnt", generic = "cntreg",
                   arg = c("y", "grp", "adj"),
                   column = c("count", "sex", "year"),
                   recode = c("", "f=1;*=0", "fac"))
e <- data.frame(count = c(4, 30, 6, 41), sex = c("f", "m", "f", "m"),
                year = c(1, 1, 2, 2))
cntreg(clprep(e, mine))
#> cntreg: 4 counts; reference 0
#> rate ratios (95% intervals):
#>   fit term       irr         lo        hi            p   sep
#>  pois    1 0.1408451 0.07265014 0.2730529 6.508047e-09 FALSE
#>    nb    1 0.1408451 0.07265012 0.2730530 6.508132e-09 FALSE
#> negative binomial theta 19990669; AIC Poisson 23.74163, negative binomial 25.74164
